title: The Glassmakers of Murano
sourceNote: Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử thủ công và nghề thủy tinh Venice.

sections.text: For several centuries, the finest glass in Europe came from a small island in the lagoon of Venice. Murano's glassmakers produced goblets, chandeliers, beads and mirrors of a quality that no one else could match, and their work was sought after by kings, popes and wealthy merchants across the continent. The industry made Venice rich, and the Venetian authorities went to extraordinary lengths to protect it. Today, Murano glass remains famous throughout the world, but the island's ancient craft faces challenges its founders could never have imagined. Glassmaking skills were often passed from one generation to the next, and some workshops on the island can trace their history back for centuries.

Glassmaking had been practised in Venice since at least the tenth century. In 1291, however, the government of the Republic ordered that most of the city's glass furnaces be moved to Murano. One reason was safety: glassmaking requires furnaces that burn day and night at very high temperatures, and in a city built largely of wood, the risk of fire was a constant concern. Another reason, many historians believe, was to concentrate the glassmakers in one place where their activities, and their valuable technical secrets, could be more easily controlled. Murano soon became home to dozens of furnaces and a thriving community of craftsmen.

The glassmakers of Murano enjoyed an unusual position. They were among the most respected citizens of the Republic, and their daughters were permitted to marry into noble families, a privilege rarely granted to craftsmen. At the same time, they were not free to leave. Venetian law forbade glassmakers to practise their craft outside the Republic, since a skilled worker who moved abroad could take valuable knowledge with him. Those who left were threatened with severe punishment, and their families who remained behind could also suffer the consequences.

Murano's reputation rested on a series of technical innovations. In the fifteenth century, Angelo Barovier developed a method of producing an almost perfectly clear glass, known as cristallo, by using carefully purified ingredients. Clear glass allowed craftsmen to produce thin, elegant vessels and, later, mirrors of exceptional quality. Glassmakers also perfected decorative techniques such as millefiori, in which slices of multicoloured glass rods are arranged to form patterns resembling a field of tiny flowers, and filigree, in which fine threads of white or coloured glass are embedded within clear glass. Such techniques were often closely guarded within individual families.

The making of a blown-glass vessel follows a sequence that has changed little over the centuries. A mixture of sand and other minerals is melted in a furnace until it becomes a glowing liquid. The glassmaker collects a lump of molten glass on the end of a long metal tube, known as a blowpipe, and blows into it to form a bubble. The vessel is then shaped with simple tools while it is repeatedly returned to the heat of the furnace to keep it workable. Finally, the finished object is cooled very slowly in a special oven, since glass that cools too quickly is likely to crack. An elaborate piece may require the work of a master and several assistants over many hours.

Despite the Republic's efforts, Murano's monopoly could not last for ever. In the seventeenth century, the French minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert, determined to end France's dependence on expensive Venetian mirrors, persuaded several Murano glassmakers to move to Paris. The workshop they helped to establish soon produced mirrors of comparable quality, and in the 1680s it supplied the glass for the famous Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles. Over the following century, glass industries in Bohemia, England and elsewhere also grew, and Venice gradually lost its dominant position.

Today Murano's furnaces face new difficulties. Cheap imitations, many produced in factories abroad and sold to tourists as genuine Murano glass, have undercut local workshops, and in 1994 a certification mark was introduced to help buyers identify authentic pieces. Rising energy costs have also hit an industry whose furnaces must burn continuously; in 2022, some workshops were forced to shut their furnaces temporarily as gas prices soared. Many glassmakers worry, too, that fewer young people are willing to undertake the long apprenticeship needed to master the craft. Others, however, remain optimistic.

explain.B: Đoạn B: năm 1291 lò thủy tinh bị dời tới Murano vì nguy cơ cháy ở thành phố gỗ và để kiểm soát bí mật nghề → dời một ngành nghề vì an toàn và bí mật: {h}.
explain.C: Đoạn C: thợ thủy tinh được kính trọng, con gái được lấy quý tộc, nhưng bị cấm rời Cộng hòa → đặc quyền đi kèm hạn chế: {h}. Đoạn có nhắc con gái họ, nhưng không nói vai trò của phụ nữ trong nghề, nên không phải {i:7}.
explain.D: Đoạn D: Barovier phát minh thủy tinh trong suốt cristallo, cùng kỹ thuật millefiori và filigree → kỹ thuật mới tạo nên danh tiếng: {h}.
explain.E: Đoạn E: quy trình thổi thủy tinh 'has changed little over the centuries' → quy trình hầu như không đổi: {h}.
explain.F: Đoạn F: Colbert lôi kéo thợ Murano sang Paris; Pháp, Bohemia, Anh phát triển → mất kiểm soát một thị trường giá trị: {h}.
explain.G: Đoạn G: hàng nhái, chi phí năng lượng, ít người trẻ học nghề → những mối đe dọa hiện đại với nghề cổ: {h}. Đoạn nói du khách bị bán hàng nhái chứ không phải du lịch tạo ra người học việc, nên {i:8} sai.

items.q: Sand and other minerals are melted in a furnace until they become a glowing ______ ↓
items.e: Đoạn E: hỗn hợp được nung 'until it becomes a glowing liquid' → liquid.

items.q: Molten glass is collected on a long metal tube called a ______ ↓
items.e: Đoạn E: thợ lấy thủy tinh nóng chảy trên 'a long metal tube, known as a blowpipe' → blowpipe.

items.q: The glassmaker blows to form a ______, then shapes it with simple tools ↓
items.e: Đoạn E: thợ thổi vào ống 'to form a bubble' → bubble.

items.q: The finished object is cooled slowly in a special oven so that it does not ______
items.e: Đoạn E: thủy tinh nguội quá nhanh 'is likely to crack' → crack.

items.q: Why were glassmakers forbidden to work outside the Republic?
options: Their furnaces were a danger to other cities.
They might take important knowledge to rival states.
The Republic needed all their output for its own use.
Other countries had banned the import of Venetian glass.
items.e: Đoạn C: luật cấm vì thợ lành nghề ra nước ngoài 'could take valuable knowledge with him' → có thể mang bí quyết sang nước đối thủ.

items.q: What did Colbert want to achieve?
options: to buy Murano's workshops for France
to stop France relying on costly Venetian mirrors
to improve relations between France and Venice
to build a glass museum at Versailles
items.e: Đoạn F: Colbert quyết tâm 'to end France's dependence on expensive Venetian mirrors'.

items.q: What was the purpose of the certification mark introduced in 1994?
options: to help customers recognise genuine Murano glass
to limit the number of tourists visiting Murano
to reduce the energy used by furnaces
to train young people as glassmakers
items.e: Đoạn G: nhãn chứng nhận năm 1994 'to help buyers identify authentic pieces' → giúp khách nhận ra thủy tinh Murano thật.
